title: The Interest-Only Cliff: The Loan Repayment Jump Most SME Owners Don't See Coming
linkedin:
Somewhere in a loan file from two or three years ago sits a date that matters more right now than almost anything else on the balance sheet: the day the interest-only period ends.

Most owners couldn't tell you that date without checking.

That's not a criticism. Interest-only terms usually get negotiated once, at settlement, to protect cash while a business invests ahead of revenue, a fit-out, new equipment, a second site. Then the direct debit becomes background noise and attention moves on.

The problem is what happens at the other end. When the period rolls off, the loan has to repay principal over whatever term is left, not the original term. Many lenders also reassess the facility at current rates rather than the rate that applied at settlement. A repayment that felt comfortable when the loan was written can land very differently a few years later, even though the business itself hasn't changed much.

We're seeing this show up as a live issue this quarter, not a future one, across businesses that borrowed to fund growth over the last few years.

The fix is simple but time sensitive: list every facility's interest-only expiry date, model the new repayment against current cash flow at current rates, and raise it with the lender before the conversion date, not after.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

A quick note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria who took out a business loan in the last few years to fund growth, a fit-out, new equipment or a property purchase.

Many of those loans were written with an interest-only period, often one to five years, to protect cash flow while the business grew into the investment. That period is now rolling off for a lot of businesses, and it is worth checking the exact date in your facility letter rather than waiting for the bank statement to tell you.

When the interest-only period ends, two things usually happen together. The loan starts repaying principal over whatever term is left, which is shorter than the original term, and many lenders reassess the facility at current rates rather than the rate from when it was first approved. The repayment can step up by more than expected, even though the business itself has not changed.

The businesses that handle this smoothly are the ones who model the new repayment against their cash flow before the conversion date, not after, and raise refinancing or restructuring options with their lender while there is still time to negotiate.

If you have got a business loan with an interest-only period that has been running quietly in the background for a couple of years, now is the time to check the date.

Read the full piece on the blog.
